implementation_notes: Python's own decorator idiom wraps callables: a decorator is a callable that takes a callable and returns a replacement, applied with the @ syntax, and functools.wraps copies __module__, __name__, __qualname__, __doc__ and __annotations__ and sets __wrapped__ so introspection, help() and signature lookups still see the wrapped function. The standard library is full of witnesses (functools.cache/lru_cache, singledispatch, contextlib.contextmanager), which is why this is the realization to bind when the decorated subject is a function or method. When the decorated subject is a non-callable object, the sibling forwarding-class variant is required, because adding responsibilities to one object means implementing its interface and delegating attributes.

variants.name: Function decorator with functools.wraps (@decorator syntax)
variants.idiom_name: decorator function returning a wrapper callable; @syntactic sugar; functools.wraps/update_wrapper preserves identity metadata
variants.implementation_notes: Python's own decorator idiom wraps callables: a decorator is a callable that takes a callable and returns a replacement, applied with the @ syntax, and functools.wraps copies __module__, __name__, __qualname__, __doc__ and __annotations__ and sets __wrapped__ so introspection, help() and signature lookups still see the wrapped function. The standard library is full of witnesses (functools.cache/lru_cache, singledispatch, contextlib.contextmanager), which is why this is the realization to bind when the decorated subject is a function or method. When the decorated subject is a non-callable object, the sibling forwarding-class variant is required, because adding responsibilities to one object means implementing its interface and delegating attributes.
pitfalls: Without functools.wraps the wrapper loses __name__, __doc__, __annotations__ and __wrapped__, breaking help(), pickling, dependency-injection by signature and pytest's fixture introspection.
Descriptor semantics: a wrapper applied to a classmethod/staticmethod or to a method that must bind late has to implement __get__ itself (the wrapt package exists because naive closures fail here).
The decorator runs once, at definition/import time, so any state captured in the decorator body is shared by every call and every test - mutable default state becomes a cross-test leak.

variants.name: Object wrapper class forwarding attribute access (__getattr__/__setattr__)
variants.idiom_name: class holding the wrapped object, implementing the protocol and forwarding missing attributes via __getattr__ (dynamic wrapper) or explicit delegation methods
variants.implementation_notes: For object decoration Python uses a class that holds the wrapped object and exposes the same interface: a dynamic wrapper implements __getattr__, __setattr__ (and __delattr__) and forwards attribute access to the wrapped object, while the methods the wrapper defines are found first because __getattr__ is only consulted for attributes that are missing. This is the form that works when subclassing is impossible - objects returned by libraries or built from C extensions - and it is what the GoF pattern describes in Python. The known limit is introspection: dir(), __class__ and __dict__ expose the wrapper, so the pattern supports programming but not metaprogramming.
pitfalls: Special methods bypass __getattr__ - iter(), next(), len(), ==, arithmetic and context managers look at the type, so a wrapper must define each dunder the decorated protocol needs.

__dict__ is special-cased and always reveals the wrapper's own attributes, so introspection-based code (frameworks, debuggers, dataclasses-style tooling) sees the wrapper rather than the wrapped object.
__setattr__ must special-case the wrapper's own fields, otherwise writes land on the wrapped object; forgetting __delattr__ leaves deletion silently broken.
